passages.t: Trumpets, and a day to be humbled
passages.happening:
The calendar comes to the seventh month. “On the first day of the seventh month, you are to hold a sacred assembly, and you must not do any regular work. This will be a day for you to sound the trumpets” (verse 1). A bull, a ram and seven lambs are offered, with a goat as a sin offering, on top of the monthly and daily offerings (verses 2-6).

“On the tenth day of this seventh month, you are to hold a sacred assembly, and you shall humble yourselves; you must not do any work” (verse 7). The same offerings are made, in addition to ‘the sin offering of atonement’ and the daily offering (verses 8-11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 28 set out the daily, weekly and monthly offerings and the feasts of spring. This chapter finishes the calendar with the feasts of autumn. The seventh month, later called Tishri, falls in September or October. It came at the end of the farming year, when the grapes and olives had been gathered. Three feasts crowd into it.

The first day is a day of blasts. The Hebrew word, teruah, can mean a battle cry, a shout of joy or the sounding of horns. The verse does not name the instrument. Jewish practice has long used the ram's horn, the shofar, whose sound gathered assemblies, announced kings and signaled war. Here it calls Israel to stand before God. The day later became Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, though in the Torah it is simply the day of trumpet blasts.

The tenth day is the Day of Atonement. Its full rite is described in Leviticus 16: the high priest enters the innermost room, and a goat carries the people's sins away into the wilderness. This chapter gives only the offerings at the altar and the people's part. They are to ‘humble’ themselves. The Hebrew says, word for word, that they are to afflict their souls. Jewish tradition has understood this as fasting and self-denial. It was an act of repentance done with the body, by the whole community together. It is Yom Kippur, still the most solemn day of the Jewish year.

Notice the order. First a summons, then cleansing, and only then the great feast of joy. The month takes Israel through a whole movement: called, forgiven, and then glad.
passages.later:
After the exile, Ezra read the law to the people ‘on the first day of the seventh month’ (Nehemiah 8:2), and the people wept and then feasted.

Hebrews reads the Day of Atonement as a shadow of what Christ has done: “He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). A shadow is real. God truly met his people on this day and forgave them, as Leviticus promises.
passages.asks: Israel's great month began with a summons and a day of honest humbling before it reached the feast. Ask whether your joy in God has room in it for repentance, or tries to skip that step. And ask what it would mean to humble yourself with your body as well as your thoughts: by fasting, by silence, by going without.

passages.happening:
“On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, you are to hold a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work, and you shall observe a feast to the LORD for seven days” (verse 12).

The offerings are the largest of the year. On the first day there are thirteen bulls, two rams and fourteen lambs, with a goat for a sin offering (verses 13-16). On the second day there are twelve bulls, on the third eleven, and so on, one fewer each day, down to seven bulls on the seventh day (verses 17-34). The rams and lambs stay the same throughout.

On the eighth day there is a closing assembly, with one bull, one ram and seven lambs (verses 35-38).
passages.hearers:
The Feast of Tabernacles, also called Booths, was the harvest feast of autumn. For a week Israel lived in shelters made of branches, to remember the years in the wilderness when God kept them alive (Leviticus 23:42-43). It was the most joyful feast of the year.

For the people first hearing this on the plains of Moab, the point was sharp. They were still in the wilderness. Their tents were their only homes. God gives them a feast for a time when the wilderness will be a memory, something they will have to build huts to recall. The law takes it for granted that they will arrive.

The numbers are worth a moment. The bulls go down by one each day: thirteen, twelve, eleven, ten, nine, eight, seven. They end at seven on the seventh day. Over the week there are seventy bulls, fourteen rams and ninety-eight lambs, and each total is a multiple of seven. The feast is built on the number that marks the Sabbath.

Later rabbinic tradition, recorded in the Talmud, linked the seventy bulls with the seventy nations listed in Genesis 10 and understood them as offered for all the peoples of the world. Numbers itself does not say this. It shows how Jewish readers thought about the number.

The scale assumes a people with large herds. Seventy-one bulls in eight days, with all the rams, lambs and goats, could come only from a settled and prosperous land. Here again the calendar looks past the desert.

The eighth day stands apart. After the abundance of the week, the offering drops back to one bull, one ram and seven lambs. It is a quiet closing day. In Jewish practice it became Shemini Atzeret, the Eighth Day of Assembly. The feast as a whole is kept by Jewish communities today as Sukkot.
passages.later:
Solomon dedicated the temple at this feast: “And all the men of Israel came together to King Solomon at the feast in the seventh month” (1 Kings 8:2).

The prophet Zechariah looked for a day when the nations would keep it: they ‘will go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, and to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles’ (Zechariah 14:16).

John's Gospel sets one of Jesus' great sayings at this feast: “On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and called out in a loud voice, ‘If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink’” (John 7:37).
passages.asks: God gave a wandering people a feast for remembering that they once wandered. Ask what hard season of your own life you will one day need to remember with thanks. And ask whether your gladness, like this feast, has room in it for people of every nation.

passages.happening:
The calendar closes. “You are to present these offerings to the LORD at your appointed times, in addition to your vow and freewill offerings, whether burnt offerings, grain offerings, drink offerings, or peace offerings” (verse 39).

“So Moses spoke all this to the Israelites just as the LORD had commanded him” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
These two verses close both chapters. They add one thing that keeps the whole calendar from being misunderstood.

Everything in chapters 28 and 29 is public and fixed. The priests offer it for the nation on set days in set amounts. Someone might conclude that Israel's worship was a matter of quantities delivered on schedule, and that once the nation's offerings were made, each person's duty was done.

Verse 39 says otherwise. All of this is ‘in addition to your vow and freewill offerings’. Beside the appointed sacrifices stood the gifts that individual Israelites brought because they wished to: a vow kept, a thank-offering, a gift with no occasion but gratitude. The set offerings did not take the place of the willing ones.

Israel's prophets pressed the same point from the other side. They said that the appointed sacrifices, offered by people who cheated the poor, were worth nothing to God. Fixed worship and a willing heart belonged together.

The mention of vows leads straight into chapter 30, which is about the promises people make to God.
passages.later:
The prophet Amos spoke for God to a people who kept the calendar and ignored justice: “I hate, I despise your feasts! I cannot stand the stench of your solemn assemblies” (Amos 5:21). “But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24).

Paul describes the giving God looks for in the church: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
passages.asks: The calendar ends by naming what no calendar can require: a gift freely given. Ask what you give God only because it is expected. And ask when you last brought him something for no reason but thanks.
